Architecture/simplification: keep request capabilities separate from the billing catalog

Whether a deployment uses modern token fields now depends partly on whether its name appears in `AZURE_MODELS`. That table supplies model/pricing data, so adding a price entry can change request construction: an unknown name loses `assumeModernModel`, switches token-field/default behavior, and may stop forwarding configured reasoning. No provider capability decision is required at the call site.

Please represent this as an explicit capability/default policy rather than using catalog membership as a proxy. The same policy can distinguish token-field choice, sampling support, default budget, and reasoning support instead of coupling all of them to `assumeModernModel`. This need only be a small data structure/helper; it does not require a general provider-framework rewrite.

[P2] Preserve supported native custom-tool options

`CustomTool` is strict but omits `eager_input_streaming?: boolean | null` from the pinned SDK. For example:

```ts
{ tools: [{
  name: 'lookup',
  input_schema: { type: 'object' },
  eager_input_streaming: false,
}] }
```

The existing Messages tool transformation preserves this object, but both new validators reject it. That prevents callers from configuring tool-input streaming through the new contract. The SDK also accepts `type: null` for a custom tool, which this strict branch rejects.

Please include these native shapes and add compatibility fixtures sourced from the pinned SDK contract. This can be checked in tests without adding an SDK runtime dependency to the portable package.

Architecture/simplification: compose Azure Responses directly

This currently layers OpenAI Chat → Azure Chat → omit fourteen fields → selected OpenAI Responses fields. A new Azure Chat option can consequently become an accepted Responses option without anyone deciding that Responses supports it.

I would separate Azure connection/capability fields from endpoint fields, then compose Responses from that shared Azure shape plus an explicit selection of supported Responses fields. Keep the existing deliberate allowlist approach used by `.pick(...)`, but remove Chat as the intermediate parent. This makes Azure-specific omissions and overrides visible in one place and reduces the chance of repeating the endpoint-field drift already discussed on this PR.

[P2] Make the new parsed contract usable at the provider boundary

The new contract cannot be consumed by this constructor even for a minimal valid input:

```ts
const config = OpenAiChatConfigInputSchema.parse({ temperature: 0 });
new OpenAiChatCompletionProvider('test', { config });
```

This fails with TS2322 because the inferred authoring type permits file references and function definitions with optional parameters, while `OpenAiCompletionOptions` requires the older resolved shapes. The equivalent Responses example fails on `tools`. The provider already loads authoring-time files during request construction, so this is not a boundary at which all those values have necessarily been resolved.

Please connect the new input types to the execution types—portable inputs plus explicit in-process extensions, or a typed adapter—and add a compile test for parsed input entering the constructor. The old constructor was already restrictive; the issue here is that the newly exported contract does not compose with the execution API it describes.

[P2] Use an MCP client contract here, rather than the standalone provider contract

Extending all of `McpConfigInputSchema` accepts `defaultArgs`, `transformResponse`, and `responseParser`, but Chat constructs `MCPClient` directly. Those settings are implemented by the separate `MCPProvider` wrapper. I validated a config with `defaultArgs: { session_id: 'configured-session' }` and a response transform, then exercised a mock tool call: the client sent only the model-generated arguments and returned the untransformed result. A caller can therefore validate configuration that silently has no effect.

This composition also admits non-JSON values through `defaultArgs: record<string, unknown>`: both exported validators accept `defaultArgs: { value: 1n }`, then `JSON.stringify` throws; a function value is silently dropped.

Please compose a client-specific portable schema that excludes standalone-provider-only fields, or implement their advertised behavior here. If `defaultArgs` remains supported, constrain it to JSON values. The same shared distinction will help the Azure/Anthropic contracts in the next PR.

discussion_comments.comment_body:
Architecture/simplification: prefer shared fields plus positive endpoint composition

Responses currently starts with the entire Chat contract and removes a long list of fields. Every future Chat-only addition will automatically become a public Responses option unless its author remembers this distant omit list. The endpoint corrections already discussed on this PR show why that is fragile.

I would extract a small set of truly shared text/connection fields, then explicitly compose Chat and Responses. Reusing field schemas is useful; inheriting an endpoint's full option set is what creates the accidental coupling. This would also make the supported surface easier to compare with each request builder, without introducing a general schema-generation framework.
